subject: anatomy
title: Peritoneal Cavity: Greater and Lesser Omentum, Lesser Sac, and Epiploic Foramen

steps.tx: The peritoneum is an extensive serous membrane lining the abdominal cavity and reflecting over internal viscera. The prominent quadric-laminar peritoneal fold suspended from the greater curvature of the stomach and transverse colon is the **greater omentum**, draping like an apron over the small intestinal coils.
steps.say: The peritoneum lines the abdomen and covers its organs. Suspended from the greater curvature of the stomach and transverse colon, the four-layered greater omentum drapes like an apron over the small intestine.

vis.alt: The greater omentum hanging as a fatty apron from the greater curvature of the stomach over the coils of small intestine.
vis.caption: Four layers of peritoneum form the greater omentum, draping from the stomach and transverse colon over the intestines like an apron. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: Richly endowed with macrophages, fat cells, and milky spots of lymphoid tissue, the greater omentum exhibits remarkable autonomous mobility toward sites of intra-abdominal inflammation. Wrapping around inflamed appendices or perforated ulcers, it walls off infection, earning its title as the **policeman of the abdomen**.
steps.say: Rich in macrophages and lymphoid spots, the greater omentum migrates toward sites of inflammation. Wrapping around perforated ulcers or inflamed appendices, it seals infection as the policeman of the abdomen.

steps.tx: Connecting the lesser curvature of the stomach and first two centimetres of the duodenum to the liver is the **lesser omentum**. It is divided into two distinct components: the thin, transparent hepatogastric ligament stretching to the stomach, and the thicker, free right-sided hepatoduodenal ligament containing the portal triad.
steps.say: The lesser omentum connects the liver to the lesser curvature of the stomach and duodenum. It consists of the thin hepatogastric ligament and the thick hepatoduodenal ligament containing the portal triad.

steps.tx: The free right margin of the lesser omentum borders the **epiploic foramen** (foramen of Winslow), the solitary natural anatomical communication linking the greater peritoneal sac with the lesser sac (omental bursa). Measuring three centimetres in vertical height, it readily admits a surgeon's index finger.
steps.say: The free right border of the lesser omentum frames the epiploic foramen of Winslow. Measuring three centimeters, this opening is the only natural communication between greater and lesser peritoneal sacs.

steps.tx: In hepatic trauma with catastrophic hemorrhage, the surgeon compresses the hepatoduodenal ligament between thumb and index finger within the epiploic foramen, executing the **Pringle maneuver**. This cross-clamps the hepatic artery and portal vein, arresting all hepatic inflow to identify arterial parenchymal lacerations.
steps.say: In severe liver trauma, compressing the hepatoduodenal ligament through the epiploic foramen performs the Pringle maneuver. Clamping the hepatic artery and portal vein temporarily arrests hepatic inflow.

steps.tx: Situated entirely posterior to the stomach and lesser omentum is the **lesser sac** (omental bursa), an extensive irregular peritoneal cleft. Its posterior wall is formed by the peritoneum covering the pancreas, left kidney, left suprarenal gland, and abdominal aorta, collectively known as the stomach bed.
steps.say: Behind the stomach and lesser omentum lies the lesser sac or omental bursa. Its posterior wall covers the pancreas, left kidney, suprarenal gland, and aorta, forming the stomach bed.

steps.tx: The most dependent peritoneal space in a supine patient is the **hepatorenal pouch** of Morison, situated in the right upper quadrant between the inferior surface of the liver and the anterior surface of the right kidney. Pathological fluid, blood from splenic trauma, or bile accumulates here before spilling over the right paracolic gutter into the pelvis.
steps.say: The lowest space in a supine patient is the hepatorenal pouch of Morison between liver and right kidney. Traumatic blood or pus collects here first before spilling down the paracolic gutter.

steps.tx: Cut across the kidney in this image and the two zones have different jobs. **Kidney parenchyma** divides into an outer cortex, where filtration happens in glomeruli, and medullary pyramids, where loops and collecting ducts concentrate urine. The columns of cortex between pyramids and the papilla opening into each calyx are the landmarks scans report on. Cortical thinning signals chronic damage, while a swollen echogenic cortex points toward acute medical renal disease.
steps.say: Kidney parenchyma splits into filtering cortex and concentrating medulla. Cortical thinning marks chronic damage on imaging.

vis.alt: Cross section diagram of kidney parenchyma, cortex, medullary pyramids and calyces labelled.
vis.caption: Cortex and medullary pyramids are shown in a cut kidney, with papillae opening into the calyces. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: Bedside trauma evaluation employs the focused assessment with sonography for trauma (FAST) protocol. The primary acoustic acoustic window inspects the hepatorenal pouch of Morison, where even one hundred milliliters of hemoperitoneum appears as an anechoic dark stripe between liver and **kidney parenchyma**, mandating immediate exploratory intervention.
steps.say: The FAST ultrasound exam searches first in Morison pouch for free fluid. As little as one hundred milliliters of blood appears as a dark stripe between liver and kidney, directing emergency surgery.
